question: What is the primary function of the human immune system?

options.A: Pumping oxygenated blood throughout systemic circulation
options.B: Differentiating self from non-self cells to neutralize invaders
options.C: Regulating core body temperature via the hypothalamus
options.D: Breaking down dietary proteins into usable amino acids

explanation: The immune system relies on recognizing foreign antigens to protect the body from harmful pathogens. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h1)

question: How do the layers of the body defence system function together?

options.A: They function independently without any communication between layers
options.B: They rely exclusively on white blood cells for all protection
options.C: They operate in overlapping layers starting with physical barriers
options.D: They only activate after a pathogen enters the bloodstream

explanation: Defense begins with external barriers before engaging internal cellular and chemical pathways. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h1)

question: Where do T-lymphocytes migrate to mature?
explanation: T-cells are produced in the bone marrow but travel to the thymus gland to complete their maturation. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h2)

question: What is the main function of secondary lymphoid organs?

options.A: Filtering metabolic waste products from the kidneys
options.B: Producing immature red blood cells and platelets
options.C: Storing excess calcium and minerals for bone growth
options.D: Trapping pathogens and activating mature lymphocytes

explanation: Secondary organs like lymph nodes act as filter stations where lymphocytes interact with foreign antigens. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which white blood cells arrive first at the site of a bacterial infection?
explanation: Neutrophils are rapid-response phagocytes that quickly migrate to acute sites of infection. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h3)

question: A patient with a parasitic worm infection will likely show an elevated count of which cell type?
explanation: Eosinophils specialize in attacking and destroying multicellular parasites. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is a key characteristic of innate immunity?

options.A: It acts immediately without requiring prior pathogen exposure
options.B: It takes several weeks to develop a primary response
options.C: It relies entirely on memory T-lymphocytes for defense
options.D: It produces highly specific antibodies against single antigens

explanation: Innate immunity is non-specific and provides immediate protection from birth. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which enzyme found in tears and saliva helps destroy bacterial cell walls?
explanation: Lysozyme is a chemical barrier present in body secretions that breaks down bacterial walls. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which cells are primarily responsible for humoral immunity by producing antibodies?
explanation: B-cells differentiate into plasma cells which secrete antibodies into bodily fluids. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary role of cytotoxic T-cells in the immune response?

options.A: Secreting large amounts of free-floating antibodies
options.B: Forming the physical outer skin and mucosal barriers
options.C: Directly destroying virus-infected or cancerous host cells
options.D: Producing histamine to trigger acute allergic reactions

explanation: Cytotoxic T-cells identify and induce apoptosis in abnormal or infected host cells. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h5)

question: What is the main function of the membrane attack complex formed by complement proteins?

options.A: Producing antibodies in response to viral antigens
options.B: Releasing histamine to trigger smooth muscle contraction
options.C: Puncturing holes in bacterial cell membranes to cause lysis
options.D: Transporting oxygen molecules to damaged local tissues

explanation: The membrane attack complex drills channels into target cells, causing fluid to rush in and lyse the cell. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h6)

question: What process involves complement proteins coating a pathogen to make it easier for phagocytes to engulf?
explanation: Opsonization marks pathogens with proteins so phagocytic cells can easily recognize and swallow them. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h6)

question: What happens when immune tolerance mechanisms fail within the body?

options.A: Neutrophils multiply uncontrollably without any microbial trigger
options.B: The body becomes completely defenceless against simple viruses
options.C: Primary lymphoid organs immediately shut down all cell production
options.D: Autoimmune disorders develop due to attacks on self-tissues

explanation: A failure in tolerance causes the immune system to treat healthy host cells as foreign invaders. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h7)

question: Which term describes the process of eliminating self-reactive lymphocytes during maturation?
explanation: Central tolerance removes self-reactive lymphocytes while they develop in primary lymphoid organs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h7)

question: Why are routine immunization programs like the EPI important for community health?

options.A: They induce adaptive immunity and immunological memory against common diseases
options.B: They permanently eliminate the need for physical anatomical barriers
options.C: They replace damaged white blood cells lost during severe infections
options.D: They instantly destroy all bacteria present on the skin surface

explanation: Vaccines safely expose the immune system to antigens, priming memory cells for future defense. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h8)

question: Which clinical laboratory result helps nurses evaluate the severity of an ongoing infection?
explanation: Analyzing the types and numbers of white blood cells provides insight into the body's immune response. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h8)
